source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Gastroesophageal varices that can bleed as portosystemic collateral veins enlarge.","B":"Peripheral edema caused mainly by reduced plasma oncotic pressure from low albumin.","C":"Prolonged INR caused by reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors.","D":"Hepatorenal syndrome caused by advanced circulatory and renal dysfunction in decompensated cirrhosis."}}
source_row.rationale: Portal hypertension drives formation and dilation of portosystemic collateral veins, including gastroesophageal varices, which can rupture and bleed. The stem was narrowed to collateral-vessel formation so the keyed complication is anatomically specific and does not create a second-answer problem with other decompensation findings.
source_row.source_detail: Portal hypertension produces portosystemic collaterals including gastroesophageal varices and risk of variceal hemorrhage. Current AASLD portal-hypertension practice guidance rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: AASLD — Portal Hypertension and Varices in Cirrhosis
source_row.stem: In a client with cirrhosis, portal hypertension promotes formation of portosystemic collateral vessels. Which complication most directly reflects enlargement of those collateral veins?
